audits.title: Animal Health - brucellosis eradication - sheep and goats

recommendations.text: To ensure that the central register of holdings (NHD) comprise up-to-date information of all sheep and goats keepers as required in Article 7 and Section D.1 of the Annex of Regulation (EC) No 21/2004.

citations.text: There are sheep and goats herds (holdings) that are not registered in the NHD, which is not in line with Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 21/2004. In one RU visited, the audit team was informed that small herds, keeping 5 to 10 animals, were not registered. These represented 10% of herds in that RU (around 150 to 200 herds). No action was implemented by the RVD to address this issue.

The amount of herds and animals excluded from the Programme, without any on-the- spot verification, compromise seriously the reliability of the data used for planning, monitoring and evaluation of the effectiveness of the Programme measures.

recommendations.text: To ensure that remaining animals in a positive flock are subject without delay, to an official brucellosis test, as required by the Article 3(13)(c) and Article 5(5)of Council Decision 90/242/EC. Recommendation based on conclusions No:.79.

citations.text: In the vaccination zone there is no additional testing of animals (both males and females) in infected herd to speed up the detection and removal of all positives (so to reduce the probability of spread) or to confirm that the disease has been eliminated. Although not required in the Programme, such testing is required in the Article 3(13)(c) and Article 5(5)of Council Decision 90/242/EC. The next testing generally takes place the next year when annual sampling of male animals is scheduled. The CCA explained that as some female animals have been vaccinated as adults, the reliability of serological testing of females would be questionable (due to expected false positive results). However, the fact that females older than 18 months and vaccinated at age of 3 to 6 months are eligible for testing, was not taken into account by the CCA2.

recommendations.text: To ensure implementation of movement restriction according to the Article 3(13)(a) of Council Decision 90/242/EC.

citations.text: According to the Ministerial Decision Ref 4888/130873 as well as Official Decisions on measures to be implemented on infected holdings in the vaccination zone, verified by the audit team on the spot, restrictions on movements apply to positive animals only. This is not in line with the Point 4.4.9 of the BMEP nor with the Article 3(13)(a) of Council Decision 90/242/EC, where the prohibition of exit and introduction of animals (except movements for immediate slaughter) applies to the infected flock.

In addition, some practices which deviate from the approved Programme (such as movement restrictions applying only to positive animals, absence of testing of all eligible animals on positive holdings, absence of bacteriological testing on positive holdings, no investigation of abortions, application of EU non-compliant testing scheme to classify a holding as BMOF, no restrictions of use of pastures used by infected animals). These practices have an adverse effect on elimination of the infection and hamper achievement of the Programme objectives to the detriment of the overall cost- effectiveness of the Programme.

recommendations.text: To ensure that re-use of pastures which have contained infected animals must not take for 60 days after the removal of infected animals from pastures, as required in Article 5(1) of Council Decision 90/242/EC. 26 Number Recommendation

citations.text: The Ministerial Decision Ref 4888/130873 does not require application of measures to infected pastures. Pastures that held infected animals are not forbidden to be used for at least two months, which is not in line with Article 5(1) of the Council Decision 90/242/EC. None of the Official Decisions verified by the audit team included a requirement as regards pastures used by animals from infected herds. 5.3.6.2 Slaughter of positive animals

In addition, some practices which deviate from the approved Programme (such as movement restrictions applying only to positive animals, absence of testing of all eligible animals on positive holdings, absence of bacteriological testing on positive holdings, no investigation of abortions, application of EU non-compliant testing scheme to classify a holding as BMOF, no restrictions of use of pastures used by infected animals). These practices have an adverse effect on elimination of the infection and hamper achievement of the Programme objectives to the detriment of the overall cost- effectiveness of the Programme.

recommendations.text: To ensure that milk from animals from an infected herd, used on the same or 6. other holdings undergo adequate heat treatment or is subject to other risk reduction measures as set in Annex III, Section IX, Chapter I, Paragraphs 3 to 5 of the Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Also, ensure that measures as required in Article 3(13) of the Council Decision 90/242/EC are applied as regards the use of milk from infected animals. To ensure that all designated laboratories start the accreditation procedures, as required by Article 18 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 2076/2005.

citations.text: Milk from vaccinated animals on infected holdings is considered as milk from non- infected animals. According to the Article 16(7) of the Ministerial Decision Ref. 4888/130873, milk from non-infected animals from an infected holding has to be used according to the provisions of Annex III, Section IX, Chapter I, Paragraphs 3 to 5 of the Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. However, no Official Decisions reviewed by the audit team, imposed restrictions or requirements regarding the use of milk from animals from the infected holding on the same or other holdings. Also, Official Decisions reviewed, did not specify any restrictions as regards the use of milk from infected animals as mentioned in Point 4.4.9 of the approved Programme and Article 3(13) of the Council Decision 90/242/EC. 5.3.6.5 Epidemiological investigation

The absence of measures as regards the use of milk from animals in an infected holding on the same or on another holding in the vaccination zone, prevent minimisation of possible risk of infection of humans or animals. This is in particular relevant for infected herds where vaccination coverage is low.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the crisis unit (NDCC) provides full coordination of all measures necessary to ensure eradication of the disease as quickly as possible, as required in Article 8 (2) and Point 1 of Annex IV to Directive 92/119/EEC.

citations.text: The NDCC was not formally established as a crisis unit after the confirmation of the first LSD outbreak, contrary to provisions of Article 8 (2) and Point 1 of Annex IV to Directive 92/119/EEC.

The failure to activate and make the NDCC fully operational prevented the maximum use of resources and the responsibility of crisis management was not shared among all relevant stakeholders. The fact that not all stakeholders exercised their advisory or management role, as foreseen in the contingency plan, resulted in additional pressure and responsibility on veterinary staff who mainly worked alone and under difficult circumstances. The absence of strategic planning at central level and of emergency funds, together with the inadequate preparedness for emergency vaccination, imposed additional burden on local services and other staff directly involved in the crisis operations and delivery on-the-spot. This most likely reduced the effectiveness of the emergency response to prevent the spread of LSD virus at the early stages of the epidemic.

recommendations.text: To estimate the amount of vaccine against LSD required in the event of recourse to emergency vaccination, in particular to address the needs in the part of the country outside the current restriction zone, as required in Point 9 of Annex IV to Directive 92/119/EEC.

citations.text: The contingency plan does not include details for the implementation of emergency vaccination nor details on the quantity of vaccine estimated to be required in the event of recourse to emergency vaccination against a disease crisis. This is not in line with Point 9 of Annex IV to Directive 92/119/EEC. 5.1.2 Activation of the contingency plan at national level

recommendations.text: Ensure that there is efficient and effective coordination between all CAs as required by Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The eight RCPPQCs are tasked with the coordination of the DREVs in their jurisdiction. The RCPPQCs draw up the annual programme of regular on-site inspections jointly with the competent DREVs. However the audit team was informed that such activities had not yet been implemented at the time of the audit (see paragraph 17). Conclusions on Competent Authorities

CAs are designated and their tasks are described in legislation. Coordination of controls by RCPPQCs is not implemented for the PDO/PGI wine sector products with a risk that relevant control requirements are not fulfilled. . 5 5.2.2 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 90 of Regulation (EU) No. 1306/2013. Articles 25 and 26 of Regulation (EC) No 607/2009. Findings Primary producers for PDO/PGI wine sector products

The national legislation requires that in relation to PGI wines, at least 20% of applications for certifications have to be sampled and analysed as well as at least 20% of the total production quantity of the PGI wine in the relevant regional unit. Given that there is no coordination being undertaken by the RCPPQCs, the audit team could not determine whether or not these requirements were met. In the particular DREVs visited, the inspectors met stated that these requirements had not yet been met.

Although the majority of inspectors met were knowledgeable on oenology, at the time of the observed inspections, there were no obvious guidelines or checklists used by the inspectors. Subsequently, the CCA stated that guidelines and checklists were provided by an implementing circular to the DREVs which were provided to the audit team. There was however no further explanation provided to the audit team as to why these guidance documents were not used by the inspectors observed. During two site visits the audit team requested traceability exercises to be performed. Although these were undertaken satisfactorily, the information of the producer, both in electronic and paper format, were fragmented and required a lot of effort and manpower to complete such traceability exercises.

The RCPPQCs visited had not implement a risk based approach to controls and neither was there any coordination of the DREVs in place. In addition, any communication between DREVs was informal and undertaken on an ad hoc basis. Controls on the Market: (visit to supermarket)

recommendations.text: To ensure that physical checks are carried out only in registered establishments in line with Article 6(1) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and which respect appropriate hygiene conditions in line with Article 16(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in all Designated Points of Entries (DPEs).

citations.text: At the Pireas port DPE the identity and physical checks take place in the operators' warehouses within the port area. The competent authority informed the audit team that the aforementioned warehouses are not registered as required under Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. The audit team noted that an adequate level of hygiene was maintained in the warehouse during the unloading and sampling of consignments. 3 In their response to the draft report the competent authorities noted that a draft proposal (common ministerial decision) has been prepared by the Directorate of Veterinary Care, Drugs and Extension Care with the contribution of the Animal Health Directorate. 8

At the Thessaloniki port DPE the audit team visited the two dedicated areas where competent authorities perform sampling of products of non-animal origin: The warehouse which is used for sampling fresh fruits/vegetables under enhanced controls is not officially controlled for hygiene conditions as an establishment handling food in the meaning of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and there is no dedicated hygienic area for food products. Therefore, non-food products (e.g. coal) would be stored together with fresh fruits/vegetables. The floor is tarmac and not possible to clean and disinfect, and there are no procedures in place to ensure pest control. In the case of the sheltered open space, which is used for sampling of products of non-animal origin (other than fresh fruits/vegetables), there is no hygienic area to 9 ensure the protection of products during unloading from the weather conditions (i.e. wind, rain) and birds (i.e. pigeons). Both locations for sampling used by Thessaloniki port DPE do not comply with the general hygiene requirements under Article 16(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 nor with the requirements of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) 669/2009. The current practice can cause an immediate and serious threat to food safety4. The above described issue was also identified by the audit DG(SANCO) 2012-6275. In response to the recommendation, the competent authority stated that the tender for the new facilities to be constructed had been announced 10 days prior to this audit visit.

At Athens airport DPE shared facilities ensuring an adequate hygiene standard are used for the DPE and phytosanitary border controls implementing Article 15(2) of Regulation 882/2004. The competent authority stated that detained consignments awaiting laboratory test results are temporarily stored in the operators' warehouse within the airport area. The audit team did not visit the warehouse since the competent authority stated that the aforementioned warehouse is not registered under Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Conclusions on the general requirements regarding the control system

Minor deficiencies were noted in the BIP facilities visited. The competent authorities make efficiency gains by allowing DPEs and BIPs to share their facilities, although some controls are carried out in establishments that are not registered. The official controls of products of non-animal origin subject to enhanced controls are not always carried out under appropriate hygiene conditions.

recommendations.text: To ensure a consistent implementation of official controls at BIPs and DPEs, in particular by providing staff with the information and instructions referred to in Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The AHD drafted the monitoring plan including sampling instructions with the support of experts from the DHSFAO in 2011. However, this plan does not cover the implementation of the requirements of Article 3(1) of Commission Decision 2010/381/EC. The audit team noted that the competent authority did not set up any plans in order to ensure that official samples are taken from at least 10 % of consignments of aquaculture products imported from India presented at BIPs1. Therefore, Pireas BIP did not implement required sampling for this type of consignment (see finding 34).

The audit team noted that the central competent authority did not provide instructions on principles to be applied in relation to random sampling of consignments of hazelnuts from Turkey in order to implement the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014 to ensure the balanced frequency of identity and physical checks upon import to different DPEs in Greece2.

There is a system for providing information and instructions to BIPs and DPEs, which supports the implementation of the enhanced controls. The absence of sufficiently detailed documented procedures (instructions) in certain areas allows for local interpretation of the legislation and in some cases lack of controls (sampling). 4 In its reply to the request of the audit team during the closing meeting, the Ministry of Rural Development and Food promptly provided information to the Commission services on actions taken in order to ensure the hygiene conditions during physical checks at Thessaloniki port DPE. The authorities will use the covered facilities within the Thessaloniki port until the construction of a new DPE. 10

At Pireas BIP: Pireas BIP is the only BIP where consignments of aquaculture products from India are imported into Greece. The audit team noted that aquaculture products imported from India and intended for human consumption were not sampled contrary to the requirements of Article 3(1) of Decision 2010/381/EC. The BIP manual or other instructions issued by the central competent authority do not include specific requirements for the sampling of the aforementioned products (see finding 5). Although, the copy of Decision 2010/381/EC was available at the BIP, the staff of Pireas BIP did not take samples for the laboratory tests. The audit team noted that Pireas BIP staff have developed an Excel table, which is used for recording enhanced controls and allows staff to implement sampling at the required frequency and for the appropriate analytes, but it was not used for aquaculture products from India.

At Athens airport BIP: The BIP receives consignments of fishmeal from Japan, which until 9 January 2016 were subject to the special conditions laid down in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 322/2014. Article 10 of this Regulation required random physical checks including laboratory analysis on the presence of Caesium-134 and Caesium-137. The testing was not implemented on any consignment. The audit team noted that the samples taken for detection of chloramphenicol in honey from China in the case of suspicion were correctly detained until the laboratory test results had been received, in compliance with requirements of Article 20 of Directive 97/78/EC.

The audit team noted that there are different arrangements between different BIPs and DPEs regarding the transfer of the sample to the laboratory: The sample is transported to the laboratory by official staff in the case of Pireas port BIP and DPE, and Thessaloniki BIP. Peplos BIP and Kipi Evrou DPEs use a courier service to transport samples. The samples are packaged into an additional box before transportation to the laboratory. At Thessaloniki port DPE, the sample is handed to the handling agent who gives it to a courier service to take it to the laboratory. This practice does not exclude the possibility of the sample being tampered with therefore it does not guarantee the legal and analytical validity of the sample required by Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

There is an adequate system allowing the implementation of identity and physical checks and ensuring that the consignments are not released before satisfactory laboratory test results are received. However, in Thessaloniki port DPE the conditions under which the checks are carried out do not comply with the general hygiene requirements.

The required sampling frequency is not always respected in DPEs and BIPs. The current sampling practices (i.e. not testing for all analytes subject to enhanced control measures) 15 do not ensure the compliance with requirements of EU legislation regarding sampling scope. 5.3.4 Decision on the consignments Legal requirements Articles 18, 19, 20 and 21 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Articles 4(4), 5(1) and Annex III to Directive 97/78/EC Articles 8(2) and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 Articles 9, 11 and 12 of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 Article 8 of Regulation (EU) No 885/2014 Article 8 of Regulation (EU) No 2015/175 Article 12 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2016/6 Findings

At Peplos BIP and Kipi Evrou DPE, the detained consignments are located in the vicinity of the official facilities, and in case of rejection, 16 are returned to the country of origin. recommendations.text: To ensure the compliance of the BIP facilities with the requirements set out in Annex II to Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2001/812/EC.

citations.text: At Peplos BIP/Kipi Evrou DPE: The BIP facilities for identity and physical checks of products for non-human consumption are also used to carry out checks on products of non-animal origin subject to enhanced controls, thus applying the possibility granted by the provisions of Article 15(5) of Regulation (EC) 882/2004. A very low number of consignments of products of animal origin for non-human consumption are introduced into EU via Greece (only six consignments in 2015 and one consignment in January ­ March of 2016). The appropriate measures for cleaning and disinfection after each inspection are in place. The measures put in place by the competent authorities rectify the deficiencies noted during the 2012 audit. At Peplos BIP the changing room in the food for human consumption area was put in place in 2015 following the recommendation of the audit report ref. No DG(SANTE)/2015-7439. However, staff have to traverse the unloading area in order to reach the changing room, which may lead to a cross-contamination and is contrary to the requirements of the Annex to Commission Decision 2001/812/EC. There is no changing room for the areas receiving products for non-human consumption at Peplos BIP, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(2)(b) of Decision 2001/812/EC. recommendations.text: Develop a protocol for the maximum time vaccine baits can be stored between delivery to Greece and aerial distribution, without renewed verification of the vaccine titre after storage in order not to compromise the effectiveness of the oral vaccination. Point (6)(c)(i) of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/341/EC.

citations.text: At the closing meeting the CCA provided copies of the 2017 packing lists from the vaccine bait supplier, CCA acceptance reports, submission forms to the laboratory, and dispatch lists for vaccine deliveries to airfields. These documents showed that not all delivered lots were sampled by the CCA for titre control, and no further samples for titre control were taken from those lots that were kept in intermediate storage of up to five weeks. 7 In 2017, the first vaccine bait delivery arrived on 31 March, a second delivery arrived on 19 April, and a third on 3 May. Whilst most lots were dispatched to airfields shortly after acceptance and sampling, the dispatch to airfields on 10 May included four of the 68 lots delivered on 31 March (40 days' storage) and 22 of the 28 lots delivered on 19 April (21 days' storage). The longest storage times in 2016 were 20 days. The samples for vaccine titre controls were taken within days of each delivery to Greece. There was no protocol in place defining the maximum storage time before re-testing of the vaccine titre should take place.

The results of titre controls on vaccine baits are not available until after the campaign, which means that the CCA cannot take timely corrective action if non-compliant results are reported from the laboratory. No post-storage verification of titres take place on those batches that have been kept in storage for up to five weeks between delivery and use.

recommendations.text: Ensure that persons responsible for the daily official controls on data from vaccine bait drops and flight lines receive appropriate training and that documented procedures and reporting routines are in place for these controls. Article 6 and Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The contracts specify that the aircrafts must be equipped with two electronic recording systems, one for actual flight tracks and one for vaccine bait drop locations. Bait drop data (and the planned flight routes) are submitted electronically to the CCA on a daily basis, and such data can be sent directly from the distribution consortium. Data on the actual flight routes are not submitted to or verified against bait drop data by the CCA. This is not in line with the instructions from the Commission services or the procedure described in the approved eradication programme. Furthermore, there are no records on what has been checked, when it was done, the outcome of the checks, or any corrective actions taken. The electronic data (vaccine bait drop locations and planned flight routes) from the aerial distribution are sent by the operator to a designated person in the Directorate of Technical Studies Structures and Topography of the Ministry of Rural Development and Food. 4 In their response to the draft report the competent authority stated that, for the 2017 autumn campaign, calibrated thermometers were used to verify temperatures for transport and storage. A tendering procedure for temperature data-loggers for use in the 2018 campaign is on-going. 11 There were no instructions explaining the purpose of the checks or how the checks on vaccine bait drop data should be carried out and documented. The person carrying out the checks was not familiar with which distance between vaccine bait drops would result in the desired density. Checks were reportedly carried out on the vaccine bait drop data on a daily basis. No records or reports of the checks were maintained. Gaps in the distribution were assumed to be linked to lakes, mountains or villages, but this was not verified against a map. If the bait density deviated substantially from the one agreed for the programme the CCA would be notified over the phone. This had reportedly happened on a few occasions, but neither the phone calls, nor the corrective actions had been documented. Due to the lack of actual flight line data, no checks could be made to verify that the vaccine bait drop data matched the actual flight routes. Such checks have been specifically required by the Commission and are described in the approved eradication programmes. At the end of the ORV campaign colour coded bait density maps were sent to the CCA without any comment or statement on the type of checks carried out on these files, or the outcomes of such checks. These maps verified that the minimum bait density had been achieved in the 2017 spring campaign but that there were certain areas with much higher bait densities (sometimes exceeding 50 vaccine baits/km2), which confirmed the aerial distribution strategy described by the CCA and the operator (finding 24). 12 Conclusions on oral vaccination of foxes

Documented official controls on vaccine bait storage and distribution are in place at arrival to Greece and at the airfields. Colour-coded maps prepared after the campaigns indicate that the vaccine bait density on the ground has been as planned. However, the CCA does not request all data from the aerial distribution that would be necessary for carrying out adequate comparisons of actual flight lines with the recorded vaccine bait drop locations, as required by the Commission. Furthermore, the lack of instructions and records of the checks currently carried out on vaccine bait drop data undermine any verification of such controls.

recommendations.text: Ensure, through effective management of the programme, that the appropriate age group of foxes are tested and that target sample numbers, as defined in the approved rabies eradication programme, are met in order to obtain sufficient data for the evaluation of the progress and effectiveness of this programme. Points 6(a) and (c) of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/341/EC.

citations.text: The CCA provides each Regional Unit with a target number of foxes to be sampled for the monitoring programme. The aim is to test 2 foxes/100 km2 after each ORV campaign, as described in the approved programmes. The hunters are reimbursed with 30 EUR for each fox, but the sampling is far from reaching the target levels and the implementation varies among the Regional Units. In 2016, approximately 9% of the planned foxes were shot and submitted for analysis under the monitoring programme. Monitoring results from Regional Units for the three ORV campaigns from autumn 2015 to spring 2016 showed that, six of the 27 Regional Units involved in one of more of the campaigns had not submitted any monitoring samples at all. The three Regional Units where 38 of the 48 rabies cases (79%) were detected during the outbreak had submitted less than 6% of the expected monitoring samples for 2015 and 2016. Two other Regional Units where rabies cases had been detected did not submit any monitoring samples in 2016. For the two campaigns in 2016, the targets for the 24 Regional Units involved were between 23 and 181 foxes each, adding up to 2033 foxes. One Regional Unit had delivered 67% of their target animals, five other Regional Units had reached 17-26% of their targets, and ten Regional Units had provided less than 9% of their targets. Eight Regional Units (responsible for 36 % of the targeted samples) had not submitted a single animal. 14

Monitoring results between the first spring campaign (2016) and the 2016 autumn campaign show that a large proportion of the foxes submitted for testing were less than one year old. This age group is not a good indicator for the effectiveness of ORV when tested between birth and their first autumn ORV campaign. Although these cubs would still have been inside their dens during the spring campaign a large proportion showed evidence of bait contact. It is not known if fox vixens are likely to bring vaccine baits into the den to feed their cubs. Some cubs were positive for rabies antibodies but it is not possible to establish if these fox cubs had maternal antibodies or had actually been vaccinated. No measures have been taken to discourage shooting young foxes in the summer of 2017. Fox cubs classified as <1 year old between the spring and autumn campaigns would have been born around the time of the 2016 spring campaign, i.e. they would be less than 6-7 months old. Of the 126 foxes sampled between the spring and autumn campaigns, 86 (68%) were classified as <1 year old. Of these, 53% showed evidence of bait contact (TC+) and 12% (9 out of 73 tested) were positive for antibodies to rabies virus. Of the 40 foxes classified as older than one year, 60% showed evidence of bait contact and 68% (24 out of 35 tested) were antibody-positive. 5.3.2 Active surveillance

The under-implementation of the monitoring programme, the sometimes inappropriate age groups tested, and the uneven spatial sample distribution add a high level of uncertainty to any assessment of the effectiveness of the oral rabies vaccination campaigns. The lack of active promotion of this programme from the Ministry of Environment and Energy makes it more difficult for the local veterinary services to engage the local forestry services and hunters in fox hunting, which is not part of their normal activities.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the way tetracycline test results and age determinations are reported from the laboratory is suitable for the evaluation by the CCA of the overall effectiveness of the ORV campaigns in the fox population and for the reporting of such evaluations to the Commission. Point (6)(c) of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/341/EC.

citations.text: When determining the age of foxes the laboratory would differentiate between several age groups and the same animal shot after an autumn campaign would end up in 20 different age classes, depending on whether it was shot before or after 1 January during its first and second winter. This classification follows the instructions from the EURL.

Only foxes with tetracycline lines that can be referred to the most recent vaccination campaign (excluding lines indicating bait contact in previous campaigns) are reported as positive, even if other tetracycline lines show that the fox had been in contact with vaccine baits earlier6. This could be the reason why, in Greece, the results reported to the Commission in 2014, 2105 and 2016 show that certain foxes (5-14%) have antibodies to rabies virus but are reported as negative for contact with vaccine baits (as described in finding 38), which is unexpected considering the nature of the infection and the vaccine baits.

The way the laboratory reports the age of the tested foxes makes it difficult for the competent authority and the Commission to evaluate the effectiveness of the rabies vaccination campaigns. The practice of reporting as positive only tetracycline lines from the most recent vaccination campaign, excluding evidence of bait contact in previous years, may assist the authorities in evaluating the vaccine distribution in the most recent campaign but it distorts the assessment when compared to the sero- prevalence, which is based on antibodies from any vaccination campaign. This practice may explain the consistent reporting from Greece of foxes that are seropositive without evidence of bait contact. The total sero-prevalence and complete bait contact data describe the cumulative effect of several vaccination campaigns on the target fox population and is the reporting method used by other Member States.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the diagnostic tests used as a complement to FAT, in case of suspected human exposure to rabies or an inconclusive FAT result, follow international standards. Point (5)(f) of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/341/EC.

citations.text: Methods for virus isolation in cell culture or mouse inoculation test are not available in the NRL. No other laboratory has been subcontracted to carry out these tests. Current international standards (Manual of Diagnostic Tests and Vaccines for Terrestrial Animals of the International Organisation for Animal Health, Chapter 2.1.17.) stipulate that one of these tests should be used as a complement to the FAT (referred to as the "gold standard") in case of human exposure to rabies or an inconclusive FAT result. Another alternative is to repeat the FAT test on other tissue samples. Instead, the NRL is using a non-validated, non-accredited real-time PCR method for this purpose.

The diagnostic pathway for confirming rabies cases, particularly in the case of suspected human exposure or inconclusive FAT results, does not follow international standards. The alternative method currently used to confirm the result of the accredited FAT method is not subject to the same quality assurance as the FAT method. This increases the risk of an incorrect overall test result which may have implications for post-exposure treatments of human patients. None of the rabies cases detected in 2012- 2014 had been caused by vaccine virus.

recommendations.text: Ensure that staff performing plant health checks have available, written, up-to- date national inspection guidelines and information on interceptions made by other Member States, in line with paragraph 1 of the Annex to Commission Directive 98/22/EC, as required by Article 1 of the same Directive.

citations.text: The DPPP has not issued comprehensive national inspection guidelines for import controls. The DPPP stated that, since inspectors were highly qualified and well trained, there was no need to provide detailed guidance documents, and that, moreover, the specific details of the implementation of import controls was left to the discretion of the regional and local services. The DPPP have issued translations of relevant ISPMs, notably ISPM 23 and 31, which inspectors are instructed to follow. In addition, some specific guidance documents have been issued by the DPPP, which deal with controls of Egyptian potatoes, collecting and dispatching samples for laboratory analysis and record keeping.

The audit team noted that many of the tasks and procedures involved with import controls are not covered by the guidelines prepared by the DPPP, for example, no 5 specific guidance is available on the procedure to follow when carrying out documentary, identity or plant health checks, or the process to follow in the case of non- compliance.

At Thessaloniki seaport, the RCPPQC had prepared a local guidance document on import procedures, the DPPP stated that it had not been approved centrally. At Evzonoi (the land border crossing with the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia), the RUDREV explained that they were planning to prepare their own inspection guidelines in order to ensure consistency of approach by different inspectors.
Inspectors carrying out import checks do not have available, written, up-to-date national inspection guidelines, which is not in line with paragraph 1 of the Annex to Commission Directive 98/22/EC.

Whilst observing inspections at five inspection posts, the audit team was informed by the local plant health inspectors that they do not have access to information on interceptions made by other Member States, either directly through EUROPHYT, or via other means. This is not in line with Point 1 of the Annex to Commission Directive 98/22/EC. The DPPP stated that this was due to limitations on the number of user credentials which had been setup by the DPPP for the EUROPHYT system. At the closing meeting of the audit, the DPPP informed the audit team that they had obtained additional user credentials, which would be distributed to each inspector involved in plant health import controls.

During visits to different inspection posts, the audit team noted that there were a number of differences in the implementation of controls across different RCPPQCs and RUDREVs (see sections 5.3.5 and 5.4.4 below). Conclusions on organisation of plant health import controls

The absence of national inspection guidelines means that import controls are not implemented consistently across different inspection posts, and in the case of small 7 quantities of fruits and vegetables imported through Kipi, implementation is not in line with EU requirements (see section 5.3.5 below).
The lack of information on interceptions made by other Member States prevents the targeting of high-risk consignments.

However, the Customs Service at the inspection post at Kipi stated that, in agreement with the RUDREV, small quantities of regulated fruits and vegetables (other than potatoes), are permitted for entry without being referred to the plant health services for import checks. The Customs Service defined 'small quantity' as an amount less than four kilograms in weight and explained that, in these cases they do not check for the presence of an accompanying phytosanitary certificate. Fruits and vegetables in excess of four kilograms are referred to the plant health service. The Customs Service stated that any plants intended for planting, potatoes or soil, are not permitted and would be refused entry, without referral to the plant health services. The RUDREV confirmed that this had been agreed as a local procedure with the Customs Service and that they were unaware that this was contrary to national policy. The approach practiced by the Customs Service at Kipi, in agreement with the RUDREV, is not in line with Article 13(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The audit team noted that, with respect to sampling: During inspections of consignments of citrus, lots were defined differently between the two seaports visited. At Thessaloniki, inspectors considered all lemons of the same variety, from the same exporter, consigned to the same importer and covered by a single phytosanitary certificate as a single lot. At Piraeus port, inspectors also considered the Production Unit Code as a defining characteristic of a lot, so that fruit from different Production Unit Codes were treated as separate lots, as a consequence of which, a significantly larger proportion of the consignment was subject to inspection. The DPPP stated that the approach taken at Piraeus was the correct one. This was not documented in written guidance; Inspectors selected the sample for inspection themselves and were free from interference from third parties; At the seaports and airport, inspectors used table 1 of Appendix 2 to ISPM 31 in order to calculate the sample size required to achieve a 95% confidence level of detecting a 0.5% level of infestation. The size of the lot was based on the number of fruits or vegetables it contained and so too was the size of the sample selected for inspection. Inspectors stated that due to the size of lots received, the sample size was around 600 fruits or vegetables in almost all cases. Inspectors stated that they apply a higher intensity of inspection to plants intended for planting, increasing the confidence level to 99%, defining the sample unit as an individual plant. The confidence and detection levels used to calculate the sample sizes are not specifically provided for in written guidance, but the DPPP stated that they were in line with instructions given during import training courses; As noted in section 5.4.1 above, there was no equipment to permit access to consignments at the inspection posts at Evzonoi and Kipi. It was not possible to unload the lorries carrying the consignments and so samples were taken by inspectors from pallets which were immediately accessible. During the inspections observed by the audit team, samples were collected from just one or two pallets. It could not therefore be ensured that the sample was actually representative of the consignment, as required by Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC; At Kipi, the local inspectors stated that, due to the lack of inspection facilities, it was not possible to apply sample sizes in line with ISPM 31, instead they stated that they apply a sample size of 10 packages or bundles in all cases. The audit team observed an inspection of semi-dried apricots and noted that the inspector did not examine all of the contents of each of the 10 boxes sampled for inspection. The local inspectors stated that consignments arriving through Kipi were often full lorry loads of one or two different 16 fruits or vegetables. The sample size used at Kipi does not take into account ISPM 31, and does not ensure that the sample is large enough to be considered as representative, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The audit team noted that, with respect to the implementation of the checks: Inspectors had a good knowledge of the different harmful organisms which the commodities they were inspecting were most likely to host; At Piraeus port, destructive sampling was systematically applied at a rate of approximately 10% of asymptomatic fruit in each sample of every lot inspected. The inspectors stated that this was aimed at detecting the presence of pest within the flesh of the fruit, even where no external signs of infestation were visible. This practice was not systematically applied at any of the other inspection posts visited; In the case of any suspect symptoms of the presence of harmful organisms, inspectors took a subsample for closer analysis in the local laboratory, where access to microscopes and equipment for destructive sampling enabled a more thorough check; The checks observed by the audit team at the airport and seaports included a thorough visual examination of the entire sample and were considered meticulous, in line with Article 13a(1)(a) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

recommendations.text: Ensure that plant health checks are only carried out at places which meet the appropriate minimum conditions specified in the Annex to Commission Directive 98/22/EC, as required by Article 1 of the same Directive, in particular at inspection posts at road border crossings. This should ensure that checks can be, and are, carried out on samples that are representative of the consignment from which they are taken, in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

citations.text: During their visits to the inspection posts at Evzonoi and Kipi, where there are regular imports of regulated articles by lorry, the audit team noted that: The inspection post at Evzonoi did not have any inspection facilities, including suitable areas for inspection, adequate lighting, or inspection tables, and does not therefore meet the appropriate minimum conditions specified in the Annex to Directive 98/22/EC, specifically those listed in paragraph 3. This is not in line with Article 1 of the same Directive. The plant health services at Kipi do not have access to facilities for proper storage of consignments awaiting results of laboratory testing (see paragraph 77 below). The inspection post does not therefore meet the appropriate minimum conditions specified in paragraph 1 of the Annex to Directive 98/22/EC. This is not in line with Article 1 of the same Directive; At Evzonoi and Kipi, there were no facilities or equipment available to enable access to consignments whilst performing checks. This is not specifically required by Directive 98/22/EC, however, as detailed in section 5.4.4 below, the lack of access does not ensure that checks can be, and are, carried out on the entirety or a representative sample of consignments, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(ii) or (iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC; In the case of WPM selected for inspection, due to the lack of access to consignments, inspectors could only check the parts of the WPM which were visible from the rear and side of the transport vehicle. Consequently, for most pallets it was only possible to examine one face. However, in the event that any suspicious signs are observed during these checks, the plant health inspectors explained that they would require some unloading of the consignment in order to allow for a more thorough check. The audit team observed an example of this, when wooden pallets were identified which appeared not to bear an ISPM 15 mark. 14

The DPPP stated that consignments of high-risk plants which are sampled in order to test for latent infection must be detained at the inspection post until completion of the laboratory tests so that appropriate action can be taken in the event that a harmful organism is present. However, this procedure was not followed at Kipi, where the RUDREV stated that they release lots once the sample has been taken and that several such consignments are imported each month on average. The RUDREV stated that there are no restrictions on what the importer can do with the consignment, but that they are warned that if laboratory tests subsequently confirm the presence of a harmful organism, that measures would then be taken, which would include destruction of the infected lot. The RUDREV confirmed that this would only be possible if the lot could be traced and had not already been processed. The RUDREV stated that they had taken this approach, mainly due to the absence of any facilities to store detained consignments. 17 Conclusions on import inspections

The lack of inspection facilities at Evzonoi and Kipi means that it is not possible for inspectors to carry out checks of representative samples of imported consignments. These checks are not therefore reliable.

recommendations.text: Ensure close cooperation with the Commission in line with Article 1(4) of Directive 2000/29/EC, in particular that the reporting obligations are met in relation to WPM from China, in line with Article 5 of Commission Implementing Decision 2013/92/EU.

citations.text: The DPPP stated that inspection data is recorded and stored locally by each RCPPQC and RUDREV, and not in a national system. The DPPP explained that, as a consequence of this, they were not able to provide consolidated import figures for imports of regulated articles for Greece at the time of the audit, although they were provided subsequently. Neither could the DPPP provide consolidated figures on the checks which had taken place on WPM associated with specified commodities from China, and did not provide information on this to the Commission, which is not in line with Article 5 of Decision 2013/92/EU (see section 5.5.2 below). At the closing meeting of the audit, the DPPP stated that a new national IT system was under development, which would be used to record and store inspection data on plant health import controls centrally and that it was intended that this system will interface with TRACES. 6 5.1.5 Planning of official controls

The DPPP stated that they had instructed inspection posts to inspect 100% of WPM associated with specified commodities from China which are referred to them by the Customs Services. The DPPP could not provide figures for the total number of consignments of the specified commodities imported from China or the total number of checks which had been carried out. Consequently, Greece was not able to notify the Commission of the number and the results of the plant health checks carried out in accordance with Decision 2013/92/EU for the 2015/2016 reporting period, which is not in line with Article 5 of the Decision. Conclusions on checks of wood packaging material
The failure to provide information to the Commission, on imports and checks carried out of WPM from China, limits the ability to evaluate the risk posed by this material.

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls are implemented consistently in order to allow for the verification that feed business operators` HACCP systems meet the requirements of Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 as required by Article 10 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: Greece has national legislation for the verification of the effectiveness of official controls. The DFP plans an annual verification programme in the feed sector. Verification can be done either on-the-spot (in case of higher risk) or by documentary check (in case of lower risk); 8 DREVS each year are covered by this verification plan. Since 2016, 21 DREVS have been checked. Common weaknesses/deficiencies identified to date have been: lack of resources in certain DREVS and absence of assessment of FeBOs' HACCP-plans. The audit team noted that no follow-up of the recommendations made in the reports of these verification inspections or documentary assessments have been carried out as yet. 5.1.2 Registration/approval of feed business operators

All of the FeBOs visited had implemented a HACCP-based system. Detailed assessment criteria for certain aspects of HACCP-based procedures are described in the feed manual. In most cases inspectors met could demonstrate sufficient assessment of the adequacy of the HACCP-based procedures. However in two cases inspectors stated that they had never carried out assessment of FeBO`s HACCP so far and they could not demonstrate sufficient knowledge to do during the visit of the audit team. Also the absence of assessment of FeBOs' HACCP plans was identified as a common deficiency in the internal audits of the DREVS carried out by the central competent authority and the audit team noted that these had not been followed-up (see finding 6).

Inspections on hygiene and traceability at FeBOs are generally carried out as required and adequately verify operators' fulfilment of relevant legislative requirements. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of controls is weakened by the absence of assessment of FeBOs' HACCP plans which had been identified by the central competent authority and by overlooking the requirement for FeBOs to take and appropriately store retained samples.

responses.response: The National Control Plan (NCP) for Feed of 2019 has already een issued (ref. n. 150/11033/18-01-2019). In order to emphasise the control on HACCP systems it is made clear that it is one of the priorities for the feed inspectors to evaluate the hazard analysis of the FeBO (section A2, par. 3, section B1, par. 3, section B2 par. 3 of the NCP). Moreover DFP has already organised a series of training sessions addressed to feed inspectors both from DREVS and from the Decentralised Departments ("new" feed inspectors) of the Ministry of Rural Development and Food. The training includes practical part (sampling) which is addressed to the "new" feed inspectors and also theoretical part which is addressed to all feed inspectors. On the 31st of January and on the 1st of February 2019 (invitation 1 & 2, participants list 1 & 2) two theoretical training sessions were held and covered hazard analysis issues. (presentation 2, page 7 & 18). The practical and theoretical sessions will continue for the rest parts of Greece and they will be completed by the end of the first semester of 2019.

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls are capable of verifying that feed business operators meet their obligations in terms of appropriateness of the retained samples taken, as required by the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: The feed manual contains instructions and checklists as regards controls on retained samples (i.e. those to be taken and kept by FeBOs from ingredients and final products manufactured). The audit team randomly checked some of these samples, and in the majority of the cases these had been appropriately taken, labelled and kept under control in dedicated storage places. However, in several cases retained samples of ingredients and/or final products were not available, and, if taken, had not been sealed properly. 6 This is neither in line with the requirements of the feed manual nor the requirements of point 4 of Annex II "QUALITY CONTROL" to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Previous inspection reports in the establishments visited did not mention this non-compliance. 5.2.1.4 Labelling

Inspections on hygiene and traceability at FeBOs are generally carried out as required and adequately verify operators' fulfilment of relevant legislative requirements. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of controls is weakened by the absence of assessment of FeBOs' HACCP plans which had been identified by the central competent authority and by overlooking the requirement for FeBOs to take and appropriately store retained samples.

responses.response: s According to the National Control Plan (NCP) for Feed of 2019, it is made clear that it is one of the priorities for the feed inspectors to check that FeBOs meet the obligation of retaining samples (section B1, par. 2 of the NCP). Moreover, during the training sessions mentioned in the Recommendation 1, the verification of the obligation concerning the retaining samples was pointed out to the feed inspectors (presentation 2, page 9).

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls are capable of verifying that feed business operators' labelling satisfies the requirements laid down in Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003 and Articles 15 and 17 of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009.

citations.text: The audit team noted that in the FeBOs visited, labels had been checked during previous inspections with no non-compliances having been identified. At the time of the audit, the audit team identified numerous and significant shortcomings in labelling in the majority of the establishments visited. Examples of non-compliances included: Complete and complementary feed was labelled as compound feed which is not in line with the requirements of Article 15(a) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. The instructions for proper use indicating the purpose for which the feed was intended were missing on some of the labels seen. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 17(1)(b) and point 4 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. The identification numbers of feed additives were missing on the labels of feed additives and/or premixtures, which is a legal requirement of Article 16(1)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. The use of certain premixtures containing vitamin A in accordance with the labelled instruction would lead to the established maximum levels of vitamin A in complete feed being exceeded, which is contrary to the requirements laid down in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2015/724. The exceedance of the maximum permitted levels for vitamin A can adversely affect public health (Question No EFSA-Q-2006-121). Vitamin A content in different types of complete feed exceeded the maximum limit established by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2015/724.

Generally, the feed inspectors met were aware of the guidance on labelling controls (see finding 14) but, in several cases, despite the training they received (see finding 4) 7 inspectors were not able to follow it and thus could not adequately assess the correctness of the labelling. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections

The effectiveness of official controls on labelling is seriously undermined by feed inspectors' lack of knowledge of the legislative requirements for labelling. Inadequate controls on the additives with established maximum permitted levels raises concerns on the possible impact on public health. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

citations.text: Generally, the feed inspectors met had a good knowledge of official sampling requirements laid down by Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, with the exception of the concept of 'sampled portion'. Not recording the of the size of the sampled portion is not in line with the requirements of points 5 and 10 of Annex 1 to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. recommendations.text: To update the national contingency plan, so that it contains provisions to ensure the legal powers necessary for its implementation, as required in Point 10 of Annex IV to Directive 92/119/EEC, taking into account the current administrative structure and organisation of the local official veterinary services.

citations.text: The Commission audit report DG(SANTE)/2015-7508 MR Final states several deficiencies related to the contingency plan, e.g. it does not contain: all relevant provisions to ensure the legal powers necessary for its implementation, detailed information on staff involved in control measures, their skills and their responsibilities, a register of staff that may be called upon nor a clear procedure for emergency staffing to deal with an animal disease crisis. These deficiencies have not yet been addressed.

The contingency plan is outdated and thus it does not reflect the current structure and competences of both central and local veterinary services. This precludes better identification of rules and responsibilities of all services in delivery of the on-the-spot operations. As stated in the 2015 Commission report, it also resulted in the absence of 8 involvement of most major stakeholders during epidemic situation.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the all bovines are vaccinated, in accordance with the instructions of the manufacturer of the vaccine used, within the area where vaccination is implemented, as required in point 1(a) of Annex II of Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/2008.

citations.text: The map below shows the vaccination status at the time of the audit: 10 Vaccination Campaign Regional Units Bovine Population 3rd completed or in progress 17% 33 % 2nd completed or in progress 33% 44% 1st completed 22% 5% 1st initial vaccination campaign 28% 18% in progress Some areas are completing the third vaccination campaigns whereas others have not been vaccinated even once. The first vaccination round is still in progress in the majority of the Greek islands and in some Regional Units in the southern part of the mainland. Those areas have very low vaccination coverage (animal and farm-level) and are below a value sufficient for protection of animals/herds (at least 95% of herds representing at least 80% of cattle population protected). They represent 28 % of Regional Units with 18% of the bovine population. Therefore, the current vaccination coverage is not in line with point 1 (a) of Annex II to Decision (EU) 2016/2008, which requires vaccination of all bovine animals within the vaccination area. Most of the unvaccinated farms in the mainland are free grazing beef herds living in the mountains which are difficult to be gathered for vaccination. The central authority stated that there is a lack of farmers' cooperation as regards vaccination of their herds in those regions. 11

The vaccination coverage varies amongst the regions, with good level of protection in northern and central parts of the country. The herd and in-herd values of the vaccination coverage in the southern part of mainland and the majority of the islands is very low, 14 therefore representing a risk of the rapid spread of LSD when entering those regions.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the computerised database referred to in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 contains information on the movements of animals to and from all holdings (including assembly centres, common pastures or other gathering points), and is able to supply at any time, a list of all changes of holding for each animal of the bovine species starting from the holding of birth (in particular, information on death of animals), as required by Article 14 (C) 3 of Directive 64/432/EEC.

citations.text: In one Regional Unit visited, the audit team noted that there were some discrepancies between the number of cattle in the central bovine database and the number of animals present on a holding during vaccination. The central bovine database contained many animals born before 2000; these animals represented up to 10 % of all registered animals over 6 months in this Regional Unit. Those animals were not vaccinated. The Regional Unit staff considered these animals as "dead". The true vaccination coverage of individual animals in the Regional Unit is estimated by the authorities as 10 % higher than the one based on data in the vaccination database. 12 The authority stated that these "dead" bovines have not been effectively cleaned up from the central bovine database in recent years. The official controls related to compliance with identification and registration rules were not carried out in the Regional Units visited contrary to the EU requirements and the vaccination campaign did not result in improvement of quality of data in the central bovine database for one Regional Unit visited4. Therefore, the requirements of Article 14.C(3) of Directive 64/432/EEC ("The database must be able to supply the following particulars at any time: - a list of all changes of holding for each animal of the bovine species...") were not provided.

The vaccination campaign effectively contributed to stopping the epizootic in 2017. The controls over vaccine distribution and implementation were good. In particular, the vaccination database is an effective tool for monitoring vaccination progress, and it allows the competent authority to assess and thoroughly analyse the situation and to act when needed. The true vaccination coverage is distorted due to the presence of non- vaccinated bovines ­ which in practice might be dead- in the central bovine database.

The pastures are not individually registered in the central bovine database under unique registration number. Instead, only the name of village/municipalities where the pasture is located is entered at the time of each movement. This is not fully in line with the requirements specified in Article 14 C(3) of Directive 64/432/EEC, as regards information required to be provided in a computer database. The competent authority informed on actions taken to address this deficiency with a proposed deadline of June 2018 when all pastures will be duly identified and registered in the central bovine database.

As stated in Commission report DG(SANTE)/2015-7508 MR Final, the central authority did not have full information on the activities on dealers' premises. The central authority informed that dealers are registered in the central bovine database. The cattle database does not allow the identification of registered dealers unless they are specifically flagged (tick box used for two options; one for dealer type A, second for dealer type B); at the time of the audit only three dealers have been flagged. When reviewing available investigation reports, the audit team noted that there were several animal traders operating in affected areas. From the records available, it was not clear if those dealers had premises (according to the national legislation type A dealers) or not (type B dealers). There was no evidence that those traders (at least type A) were registered in the central bovine database. In the reports they were identified only by their names but not by 5 In their response to the draft report, the CA stated that the central competent authority is constantly stressing the need to correctly fill in the health certificates and follow the correct procedures for moving the animals. Responsibility for this lies with the local veterinary authorities. According to our latest information, the situation has significantly improved in this particular Regional Unit which displayed the discrepancies mentioned in this finding. 18 registration number, therefore making any further bovine tracing in the central bovine database very cumbersome.

The central competent authority indicated its intention to update the existing list of approved dealers (both type A-with establishments-and type B-without establishments), in line with Presidential Decree 308/2000, in order to ensure full control over their activities. Ministerial Decision detailing the approval process is in draft stage. Once the Ministerial Decision is in place, the central authority plans to set a deadline for 30 June 2018 by which all dealers need to register online. Until then the information specified in Article 14 C(3) of Directive 64/432/EEC is not provided in a computer database. This practice is also not in line with the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 as regards notification and registration of all movements to ensure full traceability of bovine animals.

The fact that movement restrictions are largely implemented in line with EU requirements gives certain guarantees that the disease will not spread due to movent of animal. However, there controls over unregistered movements through possible "intermediate points" (e.g. dealer premises) are still insufficient to give adequate assurance that the infection will not spread by these. The competent authorities addressed the lack of verification of vaccination status, incomplete health certificates and the limited authority access to information in the central bovine database.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: The internal audit system of the DACA was not fully operational at the time of the DG SANTE audit and, so far, had only carried four pilot audits (two in relation to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004) in 2017.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: According to the MRDF the internal audit system for PPP is planned to be operational by the end of 2019. The fact that the audit arrangements had not yet been put in place did not allow the DG SANTE audit team to evaluate the audit arrangements. Conclusions

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: Responsibility for auditing of official controls has been clearly allocated, but so far only 7 EFET has put internal audit arrangements in place and carries out audits. Audit systems of MRDF are at an early stage of development and, therefore, cannot provide assurance that official controls are carried out as intended and that instructions or guidelines given to staff carrying out the controls are followed.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA stated that the travel budget for 2018 was 1400 Euro and the budget allocated for the first three months of 2018 had to be completely spent before the additional funding is made available. The Director of DACA stated that this amount did only allow performance of even one full audit per year per department and that the administrative rules put additional burdens on the audit body regarding the planning and performance of audits. For example, for the animal by-product pilot audit of 2017 the RU of Attica was selected as the budget available to the audit service was not sufficient in order to visit the RU initially planned for. DACA stated that also the number of staff was not sufficient in order to perform its tasks independently.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA carries out specific investigations. According to the Director of DACA the State Secretary may ask at any time to carry out any kind of investigation or controls and that the workload (which cannot be planned) may affect the implementation of the audit programme. The DG SANTE audit team noted that no specific arrangements are in place to ensure that no potential conflict of interests may arise from additional tasks given to the audit service.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: In the absence of a clearly defined audit universe and methodology for the identification of risk-based audit priorities (see section 5.2.4), DACA based its multi-annual audit programme solely on suggestions from the relevant Directorates of the MRDF which are involved in controls (issuance of circulars and supervision of controls) and may be subject to internal audits by DACA.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: The independence of DACA is compromised by several factors including a limited travel budget which is not adequate to ensure that the audit service can perform audits in all Regions of Greece based on risk-based planning. Furthermore, the independence of the audit service is undermined by a lack of arrangements for the avoidance of conflicts of interest which may arise from special investigations/controls and a planning process which solely relies on contributions from the relevant Directorates of MRDF.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: MRDF has no arrangements for the independent scrutiny in place, but DACA stated that it also considers organising the independent scrutiny in the form of a peer-review with another MS. Conclusions

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: MRDF has no taken steps to ensure that independent scrutiny is systematically carried out. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex of Commission Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on auditor competence: "Auditor competence and selection criteria should be defined under the following headings: -- generic knowledge and skills -- audit principles, procedures and techniques; management/organisational skills, -- specific technical knowledge and skills, -- personal attributes, -- education, -- work experience, -- auditor training and experience. 11 It is essential to put a mechanism in place to ensure auditors are consistent and their competencies are maintained. Competencies required by audit teams will vary depending on the area they are auditing within the control or supervision systems. As regards the technical knowledge and skills required by auditors, the training requirements for staff performing official controls (Chapter 1 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004) should also be considered." 5.2.3.2 Findings

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: No arrangements are in place to identify training needs of DACA staff, although its auditors have to cover a wide range of control activities. However, experts from the territorial Units can be used and for the animal by-products and hygiene of animal feed audits such experts had been used. Conclusions

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA auditors have an appropriate professional background and work experience but have not received specific training on auditing.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA stated that the audit universe is defined in the MANCP with regards to the MRDF responsibilities. Apart from this, there were no other documents or arrangements for defining the relevant audit areas and audit coverage. The objective of DACA is that each of its departments carries out one audit per year, which cannot achieve to cover the main areas set out in the MANCP within a 5-year period.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA established at the end of 2016 a 4-year multi-annual internal audit programme for the period 2017-2020 based on contributions from the relevant Directorates of MRDF. The Directorates were asked by DACA to take risk criteria into consideration for audit areas proposals and to identify territorial Units to be visited during the audits. DACA stated that the programme will have to be revised as the Directorate of Agriculture was late in delivering suggestions for audit topics and that this was the reason why the programme did not specify audit areas for the DACA Department of Agriculture.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA's planning process is not defined in terms of risk-based criteria, coverage of audit areas and geographical coverage. The 2017-2020 programme can achieve neither an adequate territorial coverage nor can it cover the areas of official controls for which MRDF is responsible.

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA has issued some notes to files with some basic guidance regarding the implementation of the audit process, but has not issued sufficiently clear and comprehensive procedures including guidelines and supporting documents, to ensure that audits are consistent between auditors and follow a systematic approach. DACA stated that a Joint Ministerial Decision, which was at draft stage at the time of the DG SANTE audit, needs to be adopted in order to provide a procedural framework for the audit system based on which more detailed instructions and guidance can be issued. 5.2.5.2.2 Compliance with planned arrangements

However, the audit reports and the statements made by the auditees met, indicate that the auditors evaluate compliance with planned arrangements. citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA does not yet have arrangements for the review of the audit process in place. Conclusions

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: MRDF is in an early stage of the development of the audit systems and did not yet have sufficient arrangements in place in terms of procedures, documentation and the review of audit conclusions and audit process. 5.2.6 Follow-up of audit recommendations 5.2.6.1 Legal requirements Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires, inter alia, that "Competent authorities shall carry out internal audits or may have external audits carried out, and shall take appropriate measures in the light of their results". In section 5.3 of the Annex of Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on `Independence', in relation to follow-up of audit recommendations: "Where the audit team makes recommendations for corrective and preventive action, the auditee should choose the methods to be applied for such action. Active audit team involvement in follow-up should be limited to assessing the suitability of the action plan and the effectiveness of the corrective and preventive action." Section 6.3 of the Annex of Commission Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on follow-up of audit outcome: "Where appropriate, an action plan should be drawn up and delivered by the auditee. It should propose time-bound corrective and preventive action to address any weakness identified by the audit or audit programme. The audit team should assess the suitability of the action plan and may be involved in verifying its subsequent implementation: -- an Action plan enables the audit team to assess whether the proposed corrective and preventive action is sufficient to address the recommendations of the audit report. Action plans should include risk-based prioritisation and time frames for completion of corrective and preventive action. A wide range of different action plans could be considered satisfactory. It is for the auditee to choose from the various options available, -- Corrective and preventive action should not be confined to addressing specific technical requirements but should, where appropriate, include system-wide measures (for example communication, cooperation, coordination, reviewing and streamlining of control processes, and so forth). A root cause analysis of any non-compliance should be conducted by the auditee in order to determine the most appropriate corrective and preventive action. Any differences of opinion between the auditee and audit team should be resolved, -- Close-out: Mechanisms should be established to ensure that action plans are appropriate and that corrective and preventive actions are effectively completed in a 22 timely manner. Procedures for verifying the close out of the action plan should be agreed between the auditee and the audit team" 5.2.6.2 Findings

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA has similar arrangements in place for the follow-up but these arrangements are not yet supported by sufficiently detailed procedures and no mechanism for escalation has been considered yet. Conclusions

citations.section: OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
citations.text: DACA is in an early stage of the development of the audit process and therefore could not yet demonstrate the arrangements for the follow-up of audit recommendations. 5.2.7 Transparency 5.2.7.1 Legal requirements Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires, inter alia, that "audits ........shall be carried out in a transparent manner". Section 5.2 of the Annex of Commission decision 2006/677 provides guidance on transparency, including the following: 23 "In order to demonstrate the audit process is transparent, documented procedures should, in particular, include a clearly defined audit planning process, audit criteria and audit report approval and distribution mechanisms. Management and implementation of the audit process should be transparent to all relevant stakeholders. In particular, there should be full transparency between the audit service and the auditee. Ensuring the audit process is transparent in the eyes of other stakeholders will assist in the dissemination of information, and in particular in the sharing of best practice within and between competent authorities. The Member States should adopt the appropriate measures to ensure their audit systems are transparent, taking national legal and other requirements into account. To that end, the Member States should consider encouraging practices that improve the transparency of the process." 5.2.7.2 Findings
