audits.title: Collect information on the national system to protect fish welfare in aquaculture

recommendations.text: The Directorate of Animal Welfare, Veterinary Medicinal Products and Veterinary Applications within the Veterinary Directorate-General of the Ministry of Rural Development and Food is the central competent authority (hereafter: competent authority) responsible for supervision and the coordination of delivering official controls of the welfare rules for farmed fish at all relevant stages of production. The local competent authorities of the regions deliver the official controls at farms and other establishments.

The national veterinary legislation sets, among others, the hygiene requirements for the foundation and operation of aquaculture establishments, regulates fish health and welfare and requirements up to the placement of safe products in the market. The approval of establishments as well as transporters of live fish is a task assigned to local veterinary competent authorities.

The competent authority has considered the Recommendation concerning Farmed Fish and formally ratified it. They have not incorporated it in the national legislation and therefore they did not issue further legal text. However, the inspection checklist includes a question about scientific protocols or guidance (including a reference to the Recommendation) used in the fish farm. In addition, parts of the Recommendation have been elaborated in the guidelines developed (paragraph 4). Those guidelines have been disseminated in the local competent authorities to be considered during the preparation and performance of official controls in fish farms. In addition, further reference to the Recommendation is made in the national guidance (paragraph 17). Other parts of the Recommendation are included in Presidential decree 28/2009.

The competent authority has developed a policy for farmed fish that identifies the need to examine the applied practices in the production with a focus on welfare in transport and slaughter. It aims to develop methodologies to enhance the existing legislation and also to contribute to the preparation of future legislation. In that context, with the support of the academia, they have participated in various projects on the application of alternative methods for fishing and slaughtering of fish. In addition, the competent authority coordinated the production of Guidelines on water quality and handling for the welfare of farmed vertebrate fish. The guidelines were produced in 2020 voluntarily under the EU Platform on Animal Welfare. These guidelines on water quality and on handling aim to be of use for aquaculture operators and the relevant competent authorities. They include factors and parameters that are common across species. The guidelines adopt and embed the Council of Europe Recommendation concerning farmed fish. 4

The competent authority considers the training of personnel crucial to enhance the welfare practices in farmed fish sector. In cooperation with academia, they have designed and implemented training for staff involved in fish farming as well training for official inspectors - the most recent ones in 2022 and 2023.

In the context of the project titled `Development of expertise for the review and update of the multi annual strategic plan for the development of aquaculture 2021-2027', the competent authority has identified the relevance and importance of fish welfare in the context of aquaculture development. Various research works exploring welfare issues are ongoing under this project. 5.1.2 Planning, methodology and delivery of the official controls Findings

The competent authority has made available to the local competent authorities a written procedure that defines the methodology for risk-based planning of the official controls. The methodology considers farmed fish as a stand-alone area, and it includes a separate tab for numerical calculation of the risk of each aquaculture establishment. Among other factors, the methodology lists the production size, the past record of official controls (existence of non-compliances), the likelihood of extreme weather temperatures, time elapsed since last official control, the turnover rate and competence of staff and the existence of certification under a quality assurance scheme. According to the methodology the farmed fish presents low risk related relating to animal welfare.

The local competent authorities perform official controls on animal welfare at fish farms in the context of fish health inspections. They use a joint checklist that includes fish health checks as well as a part dedicated to fish welfare. That part covers the use of scientifically proven protocols or guidelines to ensure welfare, the use of welfare indicators, the methods of stunning and killing of fish. In addition, it includes the verification of requirements of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 for example vehicle transport authorisation and transporter licence. Apart from the part referring to live fish transport, the other points covered by the checklist do not relate to specific legal requirements and are thus not enforceable.

The manual for animal welfare checks during transport (second version, 2023), includes in Chapter 16 specific guidelines for fish transport that assist the inspectors in their work. It includes guidelines for the evaluation of transport vehicles before approval as well as during routine inspections, for example the assessment of fitness of fish to be transported, the loading practices etc.

One of the regions has prepared a comprehensive checklist that covers the inspection of essential elements of the system applied in a fish farm as well as different process steps. This checklist includes training requirements, monitoring of indicators and keeping of records, implementation of corrective actions, assessment of the environmental conditions (e.g. density, light, protective nets), feeding practices, stunning and killing. It goes beyond 5 legal requirements but is very informative on whether and how the fish farm addresses welfare of the fish.

Although the competent authority suggests a risk-based system for selecting fish farms for animal welfare official controls, this methodology was followed only in one of the three regions visited. In two regions visited there are annual inspections of farms including transport processes and vehicles, and in another region visited, there are official controls every three years as the farmed fish is ranked as of low risk compared to other sectors in that region.

The transport operation examined during the on-the-spot part of the study, was equipped with insulated water tanks and a system to monitor water temperature, oxygen and pH. They were also equipped with an alarm system for oxygen and with backup systems to supply oxygen in case of need. for pumping the oxygen into the water tanks.

Immersion in ice and water mix (ice slurry) to provoke thermal shock (hypothermia) and asphyxia is the killing method used in practice and does not include a stunning step. Electric stunning is a requirement under the organic standard (see paragraph 21) and is also used on a voluntary basis on ongoing experimental scale by some companies in cooperation with research institutes. It has been trialled with a view to anaesthetising fish rapidly and directly after they are pumped from cages prior to killing via immersion in ice baths. This technology, which is used for Atlantic salmon and on a small scale for rainbow trout and carp, is regarded as being in line with EU animal welfare objectives as using it guarantees immediate stunning prior to killing. However, the parameters that ensure proper anaesthesia for different species and different size of fish are not yet well known, indicating that more research needs to be done in that area. Electrical stunning presents a risk to operators and requires a significant amount of investment, as it must be done in the sea, on board modified vessels that reach the cages of fish. This means that the method might be of severe financial burden for small and medium size operators.

According to the competent authority, the most critical steps in the process concerning elevated risk to fish welfare are lack of or inadequate feeding, vaccination, exhaustion of breeding stock, improper stunning, handling during selection, stocking density (especially relating to reduced oxygen levels as well as difficulties in reaching feed), impact of parasitic diseases. 5.2 OTHER MEASURES TO PROTECT THE WELFARE OF FARMED FISH 5.2.1 Research and emerging technologies ­ Other initiatives Findings

As mentioned earlier in the report (paragraph 13) there are ongoing projects managed by academia in cooperation with fish farming companies related to stunning and slaughtering of fish based on alternative methods and electric stunning. This has led to the production 6 and optimisation of pumping systems, electric stunning and killing of fish on board vessels. The results have led to the production of documented procedures that instruct operators how to perform relevant tasks, and aspects to be considered with regards to protecting staff safety, optimising quality and yield of product, and ensuring adequate levels of welfare with reduced stress of fish. For example, it describes how to collect and pump the fish so that crowding and injuries are prevented.

The main objective of the research for alternative methods for fishing (stunning and slaughtering) is to optimise fish welfare. It aims to develop a biosensor to monitor fish cortisol levels based on a non-intervention method to evaluate the level of stress. The wider goal is to deploy the biosensor in assessing the stress of fish at different production steps including breeding and fattening.

The association of farmed fish producers has published a guidance document titled Mediterranean Fish Welfare: Guide to good practices and assessment indicators. The competent authority adopted the guide and disseminated it to all relevant competent authorities. Published in 2020, its main objectives are to describe current scientific data and ethical practices on animal welfare with particular focus on the needs of European sea bass and gilthead sea bream in different production phases, in relation to improving their welfare. It includes operational and laboratory welfare indicators and lists their advantages and disadvantages. It covers different production systems, production phases and husbandry practices.

In the case of Pagrus major farms the companies have installed tents to protect the cages from intense sunlight as it is proven that direct sunlight enhances the aggressive behaviour of the fish. However, as the farmers stated during the visit, this feature reduces the possibility to observe the fish. This highlights the complexity of welfare issues in the aquaculture sector.

During the visit, representatives from the fish farming companies as well as the association of farmed fish producers discussed the main indicators they are using that are relevant to welfare. They mainly monitor and assess mortality as well as a wide range of other parameters including density and environmental indicators (water temperature, oxygen etc). They also widely deploy observations of fish behaviour during handling and especially feeding to assess the welfare status of fish. A representative commented on the importance of monitoring the acute/dramatic change of indicators, especially mortality to trigger alerts on welfare or health status.

In one company visited, the quality department has developed an advanced indicator system to monitor deficiencies of received fish in the packing plant. This includes indicators of haematomas and similar issues that affect the quality and yield of the production. The association of farmed fish producers has also developed comprehensive photographic guidance to evaluate those deficiencies, including in addition to haematomas, a range of morphological deviations (injuries, absence of gills covers, malformed fish etc). Monitoring some of those indicators is a potentially good practice as 7 a useful tool not only to minimise quality defects, as but also for monitoring welfare as these parameters could also relate to welfare. At this stage however there is not adequate scientific evidence to suggest sufficient baseline levels within which welfare can be considered satisfactory. 5.2.2 Quality assurance schemes and fish farmers' own checks Findings

The competent authorities specified three quality schemes that include welfare requirements used in Greece within their applied scope. Those are an international standard applied in farmed fish, an international standard specifically for organic farmed fish and a national standard developed by the association of farmed fish producers. All three are promoting the welfare of farmed fish, they are accredited, and they are applied on a voluntary basis. They include sections with requirements relating to welfare of fish at the different stages of production. The standards include some specific requirements but mostly generic and open requirements. For example, requirements for the humane slaughter of fish, reduction of stress during handling and transport processes, training for staff involved in the production of fish, monitoring of health, requirements relating to feeding and quality of feeding stuff etc. They also include some specific requirements. · The international standard has established risk assessment for fish welfare as a major requirement. It is asking to conduct a risk assessment for fish welfare at all stages of production from the hatchery to stunning and killing of fish and to document/monitor proposed actions to mitigate those risks. The study team considers this as a potentially good practice if consistently applied in the farmed fish sector. · The organic standard requires that live fish must be supplied with enough oxygen during transport and when kept in cages. A transport density of 1 kg of fish per 8 litres of water may not be exceeded. The water must be changed at the latest after 6 hours of transport and must be of the same temperature. The transport duration is maximum 10 hours. In addition, slaughtering of fish shall be carried out by means of incision of gills or immediate evisceration. Prior to this, fish must be stunned by means of concussion, or electrocution. The standard sets requirements for density at farm for other species (e.g. for salmon) but not for sea bass and sea bream. · The national standard includes a section for welfare. It requires documented procedures and records to demonstrate protection of fish at all production stages, monitoring and control of fish mortality, monitoring of feeding quality and quantity, feed withdrawal times, the establishment and use of practices to reduce fish stress during handling processes etc. Twenty-one (out of twenty- two) members of the association are certified under the standard. This represents a total of 80% of the national production certified. The representatives of the association indicated that they plan to embed specific 8 requirements included in their published guidelines (paragraph 17) in the new version of the standard.

Representatives of competent authorities as well as operators met during the study indicated that the use of private quality schemes has been proven to be useful to enter markets and the companies have benefited in their operations by consistently applying documented procedures and standardising their processes. 5.3 CHALLENGES FACED

Local competent authorities indicated that their main challenges are the difficulty to perform official controls, as reaching farms in the sea depends on weather conditions and the long travel distance. The specialised knowledge required for fish welfare inspection presents a challenge for official inspectors dealing with controls of various sectors. In addition, the open/generic legal requirements combined with gaps in the available knowledge relating to scientifically established baselines on fish welfare limit the capacity to enforce.

The representatives of the producers' association and the academic institute as well as representatives from the producers met, also described the challenges they face concerning fish welfare. Primarily, the lack of available scientific knowledge limits the use of indicators to protect productivity/efficiency as it is not clear which levels are sufficient to ensure acceptable conditions for welfare. They also commented that the market of farmed fish is price-driven and the competition with non-EU producers is hard to follow. This is due to increased cost for EU producers to comply with EU standards not applicable to non-EU producers (namely, in addition to welfare, feed and management of animals by product requirements). In that respect, they commented that the current requirements for labelling do not support the fish produced in the EU. In addition, they questioned whether there are welfare standards applicable to wild caught fish. They would welcome the introduction of new legislation, but strictly on a species-specific basis, scientifically based, and applicable to both EU and non-EU producing countries that place products on the European market. As the current knowledge is not sufficient to support specific indicators/descriptive requirements, they suggest the introduction of qualitative/open requirements such as the obligation to keep staff trained and up to date on welfare issues, and specific tools such as the obligatory use of root cause analysis tools and reporting on welfare issues. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The report finds that there is a system for official controls on the welfare of farmed fish in Greece. There are documented procedures supporting the official controls on fish farms and good knowledge of farmed fish welfare matters by both the central competent authority and industry. Official controls cover animal welfare in the context of fish health inspections. However, they have a reduced impact on welfare (apart from the 9 requirements for transport vehicles) as there are no legally enforceable requirements specific to fish welfare. Industry processes have several arrangements, established by joint efforts with the state, research institutes and the industry. This includes a national accredited private quality scheme, a guide to good practices on fish welfare linked to the certification scheme and a wide range of indicators already in use. Although indicators might cover welfare, they are predominantly used to ensure quality and efficiency of production. There is ongoing academic research determining welfare in sea bass and sea bream and other species farmed in the country to provide stakeholders with guidance and baselines for corresponding indicators. This, (the absence of welfare related baselines on indicators), is the main challenge that both competent authorities and operators face, and advances would help fish farmers in managing fish welfare in their farms. The study identified a good practice in a private quality assurance scheme that requires a documented risk assessment methodology to mitigate risks for animal welfare throughout the processes from hatchery to stunning and killing of fish, if applied consistently by the operators. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting took place on 20 September 2023 with representatives of the Commission and competent authorities at which the main findings of the fact-finding study were presented.

audits.title: evaluate the monitoring and reporting of antimicrobial resistance in zoonotic and commensal bacteria

recommendations.text: To ensure that (i) the development of the annual monitoring plan takes into account the prevalence of the pathogen per species and (ii) that the sampling is evenly distributed across the year in line with Article 3 of and Annex (point 3 of part A)) of Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/1729. (i) and (v)

citations.text: A review of the AMR sampling programme revealed the following: i. The planned sample sizes did not take into account the estimated prevalence of the bacterial species monitored in order to obtain the required number of isolates, which is not in line with point 3.1(b) of Part A of the Annex to the EU Decision. ii. There are limitations to the randomness of sampling, because of the instruction to sample from Monday to Wednesday to allow for delivery to the laboratory. Plans take stratified sampling into account and emphasise not repeating the epidemiological unit. iii. The instruction is to send the samples to the laboratory within 36 hours of sampling. Samples are kept chilled during storage and transport to the laboratory where the temperature on receipt is checked. iv. The circular for 2021 was issued in the first quarter of the year, however, the sampling target was not met in a number of regions (see point 20). v. There was a late start to the sampling process in 2022 (May) and 2023 (June). Therefore, the sampling was not evenly distributed over the monitoring period, as almost half of the year was not included, which is not in line with point 3 of Part A of the Annex to the EU Decision. 5

The sampling plan did not take into account the prevalence of the relevant bacterial species in order to calculate the required number of samples and did not include meat from turkey in the retail sampling in 2022, which may have affected the number of available isolates.
Late implementation of the plans for 2022 and 2023 resulted in an uneven distribution of the samples over the year, negatively impacting the representativeness of the data.

recommendations.text: To take adequate samples to ensure that the required number of isolates is subject to AMR testing and reported to EFSA, in line with Article 3 of and point 4.1 of part A of the Annex to the Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/1729. (vi), 20(iii)(a), 20(iii)(b), 23(v), 24(iv), 45 and 46

citations.text: Regarding Salmonella spp. isolates obtained from the SNCP in 2022: i. Isolates were obtained from samples collected from the populations of laying hens, broilers and fattening turkeys in the framework of the national control plans provided for in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. ii. Official and operator samples are analysed in 4 official laboratories and 29 private laboratories in Greece, designated as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. National designated laboratories are obliged to provide Salmonella spp. isolates to the NRL. iii. A total of 40 isolates were obtained from laying hen flocks, mostly from official laboratories, and were referred to the NRL. iv. A total of 13 isolates obtained from broiler flocks, mostly from official laboratories, were referred to the NRL. v. No isolates were available from fattening turkey flocks. vi. None of the isolates obtained was tested for AST, which is not in line with point 4 of Part A of the Annex to the EU Decision.

The lack of adequate sampling at slaughterhouse, retail level and BCPs has resulted in Greece not achieving the planned number of samples since 2021. As a consequence, there was also a low number of isolates available for AST at this level in 2021 and 2023. Additionally, no AST was performed in 2022, resulting in no test data available for transmission to EFSA.

The lack of information available for 2022 combined with incomplete data set for the years 2021 to 2023, raises a concern regarding the gap in AMR information and affects the representativeness of Greek data and its comparability across the EU.

The laboratories involved in AMR monitoring are properly designated, have quality systems in place and participate in proficiency tests with overall satisfactory results. The laboratory performance and reliability of the results provided can be considered satisfactory. However, the continuing pressure on equipment and resources represents a potential risk to the monitoring programme.

There were several instances where AST was not conducted on available isolates (nor reported to EFSA) due to extreme delays in procurement of laboratory consumables. This negatively affects the representativeness of the Greek data.

recommendations.text: To ensure that all required samples at BCPs are collected, at a frequency established by Article 3 of and Annex (point 3.3 of Part A) to Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/1729. (iii) and 24(iv)

citations.text: Regarding sampling at BCPs: i. Nine BCPs are designated for products of animal origin. The majority of the meat arrives in through the BCPs at Pireus, Athens Airport and Thessaloniki. ii. The BCP sampling plan requires one sample per country of origin in the main ports. This is based on the number of consignments received in the previous year provided by the BCPs. iii. Only one consignment of chicken meat from Brazil was sampled in a BCP in 2022. Two isolates of E. coli were subsequently recovered; however, no AST was performed on these isolates. iv. There were no samples taken in 2021 or 2023. However, a significant number of beef consignments and a small number of pork consignments from different countries of origin that arrived in the BCPs could have been eligible for sampling. The competent authorities agreed that there was a number of eligible consignments that should have been sampled. This lack of sampling is not in line with point 3.3(a) of Part A of the Annex to the EU Decision. 8 Conclusions on sampling framework and analysis

The lack of adequate sampling at slaughterhouse, retail level and BCPs has resulted in Greece not achieving the planned number of samples since 2021. As a consequence, there was also a low number of isolates available for AST at this level in 2021 and 2023. Additionally, no AST was performed in 2022, resulting in no test data available for transmission to EFSA.

audits.title: evaluate emergency preparedness in the plant health sector

recommendations.text: Ensure that all official laboratories involved in plant health surveys are accredited as set out in Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 or comply with the conditions for derogation from mandatory accreditation as set out in Article 40(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: There are six other designated official laboratories. These are responsible for testing approximately 6-7% of samples taken during the course of the annual survey programme. These official laboratories are: · Forest Entomology and Nematodes, Forest Research Institute, ELGO- DIMITRA, · Forest pathology, Institute of Mediterranean Forest Ecosystems, ELGO- DIMITRA, · Crop diseases, Institute of Olive Tree, Subtropical Crops and Viticulture, ELGO- DIMITRA, 4 · Plant Virology and Microbiology Laboratory, Mediterranean Agronomic Institute of Chania, · Biological and Biotechnological Applications, School of Agricultural Sciences, Hellenic Mediterranean University, · Entomology and Agricultural Zoology, Department of Agriculture Crop Production and Rural Environment, University of Thessaly.

The MRDF stated that these laboratories are not accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025, and that they do not meet all the criteria set out in Article 40(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 that an official laboratory must comply with to avail of the derogation from the condition for mandatory accreditation. Specifically, they do not meet points (iii) and (iv) of Article 40(1)(b) of the same Regulation relating to comparative or proficiency testing and having a quality assurance system. Conclusions on Competent Authorities

The available laboratory capacity provides sufficient support to the CAs for the early detection of relevant priority pests. However, a small proportion of samples are tested in official laboratories which are neither accredited, nor meeting the criteria for the derogation from accreditation, which increases the risk that results from these laboratories may not be accurate.

recommendations.text: Ensure that surveys are carried out on all relevant Union quarantine pests (including relevant priority pests) in line with the multi-annual survey plan so that legally required work on surveys can be completed in line with Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and Article 2 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201.

citations.text: In 2022 and 2023, the CAs completed approximately; · 70% of the planned number of visual examinations for X. fastidiosa, · 103% and 86% of the planned number of plant samples and 78% and 44% of the planned number of vector samples for X. fastidiosa, · 70% of the planned number of visual examinations, plant samples and vector samples. for C. Liberibacter spp, · 84% and 96% of the planned number of traps for B. dorsalis.

Fifty-eight per-cent of the planned number surveys were completed, 60% of the planned number of samples taken, and 77% of the planned number of traps placed for all pests in the annual survey programmes for 2022 and 2023. The MRDF stated that while the DRDIs meet their survey targets each year, the DREVs consistently fail to implement the planned number of surveys allocated to them. The MDRF attributes this due to the low priority which DREVs give to plant health survey work, rather than insufficient staff resources. The MRDF and BPI monitor implementation of the survey programme on an ongoing basis, and when implementation falls behind schedule, MRFD issues letters to the DREVs to emphasise the importance of completing the survey programme. MRDF stated that these letters help to improve the performance of the DREVs.

The BPI estimates that in 2025 (Year 2 of the multi-annual survey programme), the survey workload will increase by 15% and by a further 20% in 2026 (Year 3). The MRFD and the BPI acknowledged that this is very likely to mean that the percentage of planned surveys completed will decline in both years, in the absence of additional resources.

Greece does not conduct surveys for priority pests in line with the requirements of Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and for all relevant Union quarantine pests in line with the requirements of Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Finally, it does not conduct surveys for X. fastidiosa in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. This is because while surveys are conducted by knowledgeable inspectors, at appropriate locations and appropriate times, the DREVs consistently fail to implement a sufficiently high number of visual examinations, sampling and testing as appropriate for each priority pest, and as outlined in the annual survey programmes, as required by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Reporting surveys

The consistent failure to complete all planned surveys, and the likelihood that this problem will worsen in the course of the current multi-annual survey programme, means that any outbreaks of relevant Union quarantine pests (including relevant priority pests) may not be detected promptly.

recommendations.text: Ensure that: all required contingency plans are drawn up and kept up to date, and communicated to the Commission and to other MS, as required by Article 25(1), (4) and (5) of Regula- tion (EU) 2016/2031, simulation exercises are carried out for all relevant priority pests within a reasonable period of time in accordance with Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

citations.text: Greece had not drawn up all required contingency plans nor had they been communicated to the Commission and other MS and published on the internet by 14 December 2023 contrary to Article 25(1), (4) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Greece completed and provided 11 contingency plans to the Commission just a few weeks prior to this audit in October 2024. The MRDF stated that a further four plans would be finalised by the end of 2024, and that the final four plans would be completed in 2025.

Given that Greece only completed the first 11 of the 19 required contingency plans in the weeks prior to the audit, it did not have an opportunity to carry out simulation exercises concerning the implementation of the contingency plans as required by Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 by the time of the audit in October 2024. Conclusions on contingency plans

Greece has yet to complete the required contingency plans for relevant priority pests, or to undertake any simulation exercises concerning their implementation. This raises doubts that Greece is sufficiently prepared to take effective actions to eradicate any outbreaks of priority pests, in line with EU requirements.

recommendations.text: Ensure that competent authorities have access to a sufficient number of suitably 2. qualified staff as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 in order to conduct movement controls with a required frequency and implement surveys inside demarcated areas in line with Article 7 and 11 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 respectively Ensure that official inspections are carried during the three months period prior to movement as required by Article 11(1)(a)(ii) and 11(1)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134

citations.text: The number of DREV staff allocated for tasks required by Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 are not sufficient to complete these tasks, in particular with regard to the surveys inside DAs. This is not in line with the Article 5(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. This lack of staff has resulted in significant delays in implementing the required measures. BPI plans to recruit 20 full time equivalent staff to conduct surveys inside DAs to address this problem. While a budget of 850,000 EUR has been secured, the recruitment procedure only started at the end of May 2024, with the result that it will be, at best, a number of months before the required/planned number of surveys are being conducted inside the DAs (see details under Chapter 7.5). 7.1.4 Laboratories

The lack of staff to conduct surveys in DAs, coupled with delays in recruiting additional staff, increases the risk that any new outbreaks in buffer zones will not be detected quickly, thereby increasing the risk of the pest spreading to pest free areas.

The survey design and sampling scheme currently implemented in practice do not comply with requirements of Article 7(c) of the Regulation (EU) 2023/1134. While the survey design seeks to identify a level of pest presence of 0.8% with 95% confidence, delays in recruiting an additional 20 staff for BPI have resulted in only approximately 30% of the planned level of trapping and scouting being conducted by DREV staff. According to the survey plan for 2024, some 355 traps were planned to be placed with weekly checks of each trap. However, only 130 traps had been placed and only 610 trap checks had been done by the start of the audit. The NPPO stated that in the course of the audit more traps had been placed and that the level of trapping had increased to 45% of the planned level. The NPPO stated that some traps would be established later as crops had not yet been planted at the planned locations of some traps. The audit team noted that there were already first four findings of adult males in traps in Crete in 2024. The CAs stated that it was too early to be certain if these adults had flown in from other countries or had emerged from overwintered pupae, and therefore were evidence of pest establishment in Crete.

The NPPO stated that once the 20 extra staff are recruited, the survey target should be met, and that DREV staff could then be reallocated to other mandatory tasks. However, as the recruitment process had only started in late May 2024 it is unlikely that requirements of Article 7(c) of the Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 will be met for the 2024 survey.

In the regions visited by the audit team, the audit team observed that; 8 · 30 traps were placed in the region of Lasithi, while 46 should have been placed according to survey plan. In addition, weekly checks of traps started in late April- early May 2024. While the survey guideline from BPI requires checks every 10- 12 day in the winter and weekly from March onwards, this had not been respected for two out of three traps examined by the audit team. · 43 traps were placed in the region of Heraklion, while 54 should have been placed according to survey plan. Weekly checks of traps started in late April-early May 2024. The authorities in Heraklion stated that prior to the publication of the action plan, they followed the methodology developed for the delimiting survey; · For the whole DA area of Evia and Attica, 49 traps had been placed at the time of the audit while 120 are foreseen in the survey plan. Weekly checks started in early May 2024; · In survey sites visited by the audit team, the traps were correctly placed and data were correctly recorded in the database provided by the BPI. Conclusions on the surveys in DAs

Failing to complete the planned number of surveys and scouting actions increases the risk of the pest not being detected in a timely manner, and consequently delays the implementation of measures required for pest eradication.

In the region of Lasithi, six inspectors are allocated for the official controls described under point 37. A maximum of three such inspections per inspector per week can be undertaken due to other control obligations. Given that there are 460 operators registered for movement controls, it is very unlikely that this inspection target can be met. Similar concerns were expressed also by other regional units of DREVs visited.

Delays in implementing movement controls and lack of resources to meet the inspection targets may have increased the risk in the pest spreading to pest-free areas, given that there was significant quantities of peppers and aubergines moved out from one of the DAs from September 2023 up to the time of the audit without the required controls.

audits.title: Evaluation of the implementation of animal health controls in relation to African swine fever

recommendations.text: To ensure the accuracy and completeness of the data in the national pig database, in particular as regards non-commercial establishments, and of the information kept at registers at establishment level, in order to support official controls for ASF and to ensure traceability in the case of ASF outbreak. Articles 84 and 109(1)(c) of Regulation 2016/429, Article 3 (1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/520 and

citations.text: Temporary official veterinarians ("seasonal veterinarians") have been hired to implement ASF measures in four areas of higher risk. During their work they also detected a significant number of not registered non-commercial farms. Since 2023, the number of small pig farms has decreased significantly in Greece as many did not meet minimum biosecurity standards and a depopulation programme was put in place. Nevertheless, there are gaps as regards the registration of non-commercial farms. Incomplete entries and delays in updating the national pig database as well as the farm registers do not allow the competent authority to have a reliable overview of the pig population for animal health control purposes.

Despite a national plan for implementing official controls on biosecurity measures during hunting activities, the competent authority does not carry out such controls as planned; related activities have also not produced any impact so far. In addition, the national plan is not well established as regards scope, inspection records and addressing non-compliances. This means that the competent authority has limited control over the risk of the virus spreading by hunted wild boar.

Passive surveillance of the domestic pig population is implemented through testing of dead animals notified to authorities by farmers. The level of notifications is overall satisfactory for larger establishments, whereas absent or incomplete mortality records in smaller farms make verification of compliance in these operations difficult to estimate.

The number of reported wild boar found dead by hunters is very low compared to the hunting bag (total number of wild boars hunted per year). This is compounded by underreporting and thus a lack of testing of carcasses hunted in restricted areas and destined for private consumption. As a result, the competent authority misses important information on the epidemiological status of the disease. Although the hunting community has comprehensive knowledge of the wild boar population and its dynamics, it has failed to achieve the targets set by the competent authority for reducing the wild porcine animal population. 6

The performance of the NRL in ASF testing allows for reliable detection of the virus. In some cases, however, there have been delays in the timely availability of results due to delays in the dispatch of samples by regional units and the lab's capacity limitations over weekends.

Pig operators located in restricted zones, sending pigs for immediate slaughter are not always in compliance with requirements for movement derogations regarding biosecurity and continuous surveillance. This can increase the risk of spreading ASF virus.

audits.title: evaluate controls on residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants in animals and animal products

recommendations.text: To implement the three residue control plans for pharmacologically active substances and the plans for contaminants (primary production) in line with EU requirements.
recommendations.legal_basis: Annex II, III and IV to Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/1644, Annex I, II and III to Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/1646, Regulation (EU) 2022/931.

In 2023, 70% of the planned samples were actually taken and sampling was heavily concentrated in three months ­ between October and December 53% of the samples were taken and thus sampling was not evenly spread over all months or relevant production period. This is not in line with EU legislation (17). recommendations.text: To ensure that (i) official testing laboratories are appropriately designated, (ii) that the analytical methods used are included in the laboratories' scopes of accreditation and (iii) that said methods are appropriately validated for the analyte/matrix combinations tested.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 34(1) and 37 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2021/808.

citations.text: At the time of the audit, none of the laboratories testing for residues of pharmacologically active substances, contaminants and pesticides were (46) Available at https://www.minagric.gr/images/stories/docs/ktiniatrika_Themata/Themata_dimosias_Ygeias/entypo_epek 2023_150324.pdf (47) Article 4(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2090 and Article 35(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. (52) Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 9 appropriately designated as official laboratories by the competent authorities, contrary to EU requirements (53).

The audit team visited two laboratories, each of which was designated as a National Reference Laboratory (NRL) for specific groups of substances: a. Laboratory 1 was the NRL for substance groups A1a, A1c, A1d, A2d (dapsone), A3c (carbadox and olaquindox), B1d (corticosteroids), and contaminants (organochlorine substances). In contrast to legal requirements (54), most of the analytical methods used for testing the various analyte/matrix/species combinations were not in the scope of accreditation. For example: group A1a ­ stilbenes in liver and muscle; A1c ­ steroids in serum and muscle; A1d ­ resorcylic acid lactones, including zeranol, in serum, liver and muscle; A2d ­ dapsone in milk and muscle; A3c ­ carbadox and olaquindox in muscle, B1d ­ corticosteroids in liver and muscle. Overall, five of the 12 MRDF official laboratories were using non-accredited methods for official controls. b. Laboratory 2 was the NRL for substance groups A1b, A1e, A2c, A2d (chlorpromazine), A3a (dyes), B1a (antimicrobial substances except honey), B1b (anthelmintics), B1c (sedatives), and contaminants (heavy metals, mycotoxins and organophosphorus compounds). The laboratory is designated as the NRL for B1b (benzimidazoles), B1d (NSAIDs) and B2 (anticoccidials) but methods for these substance groups were not operational at the time of the audit and any such samples were being transmitted to other laboratories within the national network (55).

Method validations were performed in 2007 using a commercial software package largely in line with previous EU requirements (59) except for stability studies (both in solution and in matrix) required in both previous (47) and current (60) EU legislation. In contrast to EU requirements (61), no full/reduced re-validation had been carried out when any of the methods had been extended to cover other matrices or substances. The audit team also identified that in one laboratory, a non-validated method was used for determination of dienestrol and hexestrol (subgroup A1a) in liver and muscle (matrices tested in 2022 and planned in 2024).

Notwithstanding the positive aspect that the laboratories involved are accredited to EN/ISO/IEC 17025 and have successfully participated in relevant proficiency tests, several factors undermine confidence in the reliability of the results generated and thus the overall functioning of the residue control system in Greece. The fact that none of the laboratories was appropriately designated and that a significant proportion of the analytical methods used for official control were not included in the laboratories' respective scopes of accreditation, undermines effective enforcement in the event of non-compliant results being found. Furthermore, the absence of information in the control plans on analyte stability (and storage conditions to mitigate the effect), the absence of method validation data for additional analyte/matrix combinations and lengthy delays in testing, cumulatively weaken the overall residues control system.

audits.title: evaluate the implementation of official controls on feed hygiene

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently verify that feed business operator`s hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) plans are comprehensive and updated.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) 183/2005.

citations.text: In three compound feed manufacturers visited, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. In one establishment the hazard identification section of the operators' HACCP plan and the HACCP principles on the critical control point were correct. The feed inspector correctly assessed the plan. In the two other establishments the hazard identification section of the operators` HACCP plan was very generic. Several hazards were grouped and assessed together, although the severity and the probability of these hazards differed significantly (for example several different types of cereals and their related hazards (e.g. heavy metals, toxins) were assessed as a single group). These are not in line with the requirements of Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) 183/2005 and these shortcomings were overlooked during previous official inspections.

In all establishments visited FeBO`s HACCP systems contained instruction on sampling, cleaning and on other relevant procedures. However, most of these procedures were deficient or did not reflect the real procedures which were implemented by these operators. These are not in line with the requirements of Article 7(1b) of Regulation (EC) 183/2005 and these shortcomings were overlooked during previous official inspections.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and ensures that the official inspections are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. While feed inspectors regularly use checklists and guidance documents and official inspections are documented, the effectiveness of these inspections is weakened by several shortcomings in their execution. These relate to the inspectors' assessment of FeBOs HACCP systems and tests on cross-contamination. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently verify that feed business operators meet the requirements for appropriate checks of the effectiveness of measures they have taken to minimise cross-contamination.
recommendations.legal_basis: point 3 of the section "Production" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) 183/2005 and point 2 of the section 4 "Quality control" of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2019/4.

citations.text: The DAFP has also prepared guidance on the assessment of testing methods and test results of FeBOs' tests on homogeneity of mixing and cross-contamination. Although, these set of guidance contained several useful information, but some key elements (e.g. acceptance levels of homogeneity tests, criteria of adequate sampling techniques), which are necessary for a comprehensive assessment of these tests, were not described. Local feed inspectors need to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the FeBOs' tests on homogeneity of mixing and on cross contamination.

Verification of an establishment's tests to evaluate measures designed to minimize cross-contamination, as required by part 2(b) of the "Facilities and Equipment" section of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, is an integral component of inspections, when applicable. In three establishments visited, the written procedures on sampling of cross-contamination tests did not reflect to the sampling procedures implemented by the FeBOs. In two establishments the physical characteristic of the tracer used during the tests were not representative for coccidiostats used during production. In one establishment several samples were collected from the first mix after flushing, however, these samples were pooled and sent to the laboratory as one sample. In one establishment the tracer used for the analyses of cross-contamination tests was scientifically inappropriate because of varying high background levels for the analyses of these types of feed. Feed inspectors met, experienced difficulties in comprehensively assessing the procedures and the results of the cross-contamination tests.

One establishment visited used a manual cleaning procedure to avoid potential cross- contamination. However, it was evident that the procedure is not effective to prevent cross-contamination. This is not in line with the requirements of point 3 of the section "PRODUCTION" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) 183/2005. Local inspector correctly identified the inadequacy of the cleaning procedure.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and ensures that the official inspections are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. While feed inspectors regularly use checklists and guidance documents and official inspections are documented, the effectiveness of these inspections is weakened by several shortcomings in their execution. These relate to the inspectors' assessment of FeBOs HACCP systems and tests on cross-contamination. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authorities' samplers have appropriate equipment (i.e. a mechanical or automatic divider necessary for preparation of final sam- ples in case of the control of constituents or substances likely to be distributed non-uniformly in feed), and consistently apply sampling techniques ensuring official samples' legal and technical validity.
recommendations.legal_basis: Annex I to Regulation (EC) 152/2009.

citations.text: The DAFP has prepared guidance on official sampling based on the requirements laid down in Annex I to Regulation (EC) 152/2009. In general, the guidance contains 9 several useful information relating to implementation of official sampling, however, there are some key elements which are not mentioned (e.g. mechanical divider, size of the incremental samples).

The audit team observed official sampling in two compound feed manufacturers visited (the matrix and parameters to be controlled were suggested by the audit team). In both cases inspectors sampled a part of the batch (sampled portion). The audit team identified some shortcomings during these official sampling such as: · inappropriate mixing of the aggregate sample · inaccurate calculation of the weight of the aggregate sample · inappropriate reduction of reduced sample to final samples · missing of reference to the sampled portion on the sampling protocol. These findings are not in line with the legal requirements of Annex I to Regulation (EC) 152/2009.

DAFP officials and local feed inspectors stated that they do not have dividers to be used during official sampling. This is not in line with the requirements of point 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) 152/2009. 5.2.2.3 Testing of official feed samples

Many aspects of the planning and implementation of sampling and testing of official feed samples are positive. A risk-based approach has been adopted for the planning of official sampling, and the interpretation of the analytical results are correct. However, the inappropriate implementation of official sampling procedure and inadequate procedure for designation of official feed laboratories could adversely affect the legal and technical validity of official feed samples and the reliability of decisions made on the basis of the corresponding results. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

recommendations.text: To ensure by established procedures and documentation that the competent au- thorities may only designate a laboratory which fulfil the requirements as an official laboratory for the analysis of feed samples.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625

citations.text: The DAFP is responsible for the designation of the official laboratories except for medicated feed. The designation documentation of the three FCL laboratories and two other state-owned laboratories was in line with the requirements laid down in Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The DAFP has no written designation decision in place for the external laboratories, however, formal written agreements were in place for the analysis of official feed samples by both the DAFP and the external laboratories which are in general renewed every year. The audit team reviewed the agreements and associated documents relating to procedures and service delivery and noted that for the laboratories located in other Member States the DAFP was unable to provide any documentation whether the laboratory fulfils the requirements of Article 37(2)(b) to demonstrate the laboratory is already designated as an official laboratory by the competent authorities of the Member State on whose territory it is located.

For the three FCL laboratories and two other state-owned laboratories the methods of laboratory analysis used for the purpose of official controls were included in their respective scopes of accreditation to EN ISO/IEC 17025. Thus, the requirements laid down in Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 were met for these laboratories. However, the audit team noted that for one of the private laboratories, the method of laboratory analysis used for the purpose of official controls for antibiotics in feed was not included in its respective scope of accreditation to EN ISO/IEC 17025 and the testing was performed outside of EN ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation and accordingly did not meet the requirements laid down in Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Many aspects of the planning and implementation of sampling and testing of official feed samples are positive. A risk-based approach has been adopted for the planning of official sampling, and the interpretation of the analytical results are correct. However, the inappropriate implementation of official sampling procedure and inadequate procedure for designation of official feed laboratories could adversely affect the legal and technical validity of official feed samples and the reliability of decisions made on the basis of the corresponding results. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

recommendations.text: To ensure that, in the event of established non-compliance(s), the competent authority consistently ensures that feed business operator remedies the non- compliance(s) and prevents its further occurrences.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team audit team reviewed 11 sampling and one inspection-related non- compliances. The feed inspectors could provide the official reports on the follow-up of these non-compliances. In one case the reports provided sufficient information indicating that the FeBOs had carried out investigations to address the deficiency, and/or identify the root cause, and/or prevent the reoccurrence of the identified non- compliances. This is in line with the requirements of Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. However, in the other ten sampling-related and one inspection related cases, the competent authority could not provide written evidence, that FeBOs carried out adequate investigation to find the root cause (e.g. antibiotic in pig feed, aflatoxin in maize, carry over of salinomycin in poultry feed) and took actions to prevent the reoccurrence of the identified non-compliances (e.g. by modification of HACCP procedures) which are not in line with the above-mentioned legislative requirements. Conclusion on the actions taken on non-compliances

Notwithstanding the fact that the competent authority took actions when non- compliances were identified in the course of official controls, the competent authority did not ensure the quality and consistency of official controls in relation to (i) the determination of the origin and extent of the non-compliances, (ii) operator remediation of the non-compliance, and (iii) prevention of further occurrences. Collectively these shortcomings weaken the effectiveness of the system of official controls on feed.
